version.description: Semver. The bump a change needs is set by the device's lock (`device.lock.json` beside the manifest), which fingerprints shape, names, surface and gaps: a surface-only change is a patch; ids added with nothing moved or removed is a minor; any other change to shape or names is a major, because a moved slot invalidates a cached coordinate as a renamed id invalidates a held reference. Check the bump against the lock before regenerating the lock, or the change it would have reported is lost. Lint L53 reports content that changed when the version did not: a warning while the device is `draft` or `modelled`, an error once it is `verified`.

maturity.description: how far this device has been taken, and the standard lint holds it to. draft: no requirement. modelled: must carry a provenance block citing a datasheet or hardware guide. verified: additionally no dimension may be estimated. REQUIRED, with no default: a device states its level rather than inheriting one.

aliases.description: THE OTHER NAMES THIS BOX IS SOLD OR LISTED UNDER, so a hardware compatibility list that names it by an AS number, a marketing name or an OEM's name resolves to one drawing. `model` stays the canonical name and is never repeated here. Orderable SKUs are not aliases - they live in `configurations.*.part-numbers`. Every entry has one shape, an object, so every consumer reads it one way and no alias is a bare string with its caveat lost. `kind` says what sort of name it is: `vendor` the manufacturer's own other number for the same box, `marketing` the manufacturer's catalogue name, `oem` a name another company sells it under, `superseded` a name the manufacturer used for it before, `variant` a NEAR-TWIN that differs in a stated way (the `note` says how), listed so a search finds the closest drawing without claiming it is the same box. L111 holds a name to one device unless every claimant marks it `shared`, and never lets it equal another device's `model`. configs.json and devices.json publish the names only.

note.description: the caveat that keeps the alias honest - where the mapping comes from, or how a variant differs

shared.description: this name is knowingly claimed by more than one device - an OEM name mapped to either of a pair. L111 accepts a duplicate only when EVERY claimant says so

profile.description: WHAT KIND OF DEVICE THIS IS, from the classes in the profiles vocabulary, which says what a device of each class has to STATE before the `specified` capability flag is true. REQUIRED, because a device without one is not judged leniently, it is not judged at all: its `specified` flag reads `cannot evaluate`. The classes are few and each carries the argument for its own minimum set - `optical` owes no cpu or memory, `server` owes no switching performance.

datasheet.description: THE VENDOR DATASHEET this device was modelled from. A guide, manual or quick-start goes in `references:` instead - the distinction is what the document IS, not which came first.

title.description: the document as it names itself on its own first page, not as its file is named. A reader has to be able to search for it.

url.description: where the document was obtained, when that is known. Absent is not a defect: a document read from a vendor portal behind a login, or received directly, has no citable address, and inventing one would be worse than omitting it.

sha256.description: SHA-256 of the copy of the file the project holds. Present exactly when the project holds a copy, absent when the document was read but not kept, which is what makes a hash checkable rather than decorative. A hash for a document nobody holds is a claim nobody can test, so do not add one from a vendor page.

references.description: additional source documents - hardware guides, installation guides, quick-start guides, user manuals - registered exactly like the datasheet. A device may register these and no datasheet: a device modelled from its guides alone has an honest record, not a gap.

title.description: the document as it names itself on its own first page, not as its file is named. A reader has to be able to search for it.

url.description: where the document was obtained, when that is known. Absent is not a defect: a document read from a vendor portal behind a login, or received directly, has no citable address, and inventing one would be worse than omitting it.

sha256.description: SHA-256 of the copy of the file the project holds. Present exactly when the project holds a copy, absent when the document was read but not kept, which is what makes a hash checkable rather than decorative. A hash for a document nobody holds is a claim nobody can test, so do not add one from a vendor page.

lint.description: WHAT THIS DEVICE HAS DECIDED ABOUT A RULE, as opposed to what it has not got round to. The library's lint baseline records what is merely already true; this records what a person has argued. A rear vent field that L44 reports as buried, because the power modules cover it in 2D, may still be right to keep when it is what opens the rear panel in 3D once a module is pulled: that is a decision, and it is written here, where a count can see it.

waive.description: rule code -> why this device will not satisfy it. The reason is REQUIRED and is checked for length, because a waiver whose reason is `n/a` is the thing that turns a rule off for everyone who copies the device. Waived warnings are still counted and still listed in the run's summary - they are separated, never hidden.

stack-exceptions.description: A BELLY-TO-BELLY CAGE STACK THAT IS NOT DRAWN THE LIBRARY'S WAY, and why. Lint L108 holds every stacked SFP/QSFP/QSFP-DD cage pair to one convention - a row pair upper rotate 0 over lower rotate 180, a column pair (cages turned on their side) left 270 beside right 90, so both bails face outward - and this is the one place a device, its layout.yaml, or a component contract says a pair is otherwise. Each entry names the pair (or several pairs that share one reason) by id and carries the reading that overturns the convention. OSFP stacks are not checked.

pair.description: the two cage ids, upper then lower (or left then right)

pairs.description: several pairs that share one reason

reason.description: the recorded reading that overturns the convention - a photograph, a drawing, the lamps - cited, not a preference

view.description: the view the pair is in, where the same ids pair in more than one

provenance.description: WHERE EACH FIGURE ON THIS DEVICE CAME FROM, keyed by the figure. Each entry is an object, not a sentence: `note` carries the prose and `confidence` carries the word, so a rule can ask what otherwise only a reader could answer - L15 reads it, since `maturity: verified` means no dimension may be estimated. `confidence` is OPTIONAL and is written only where it is known, never guessed from the prose; L93 counts the entries without one, and the count is meant to fall.

confidence.description: the library's word for how this figure is known, filled only where it is actually known. Absent means nobody has said - NOT that the figure is weak.

note.description: the prose: what was read, out of which document, at what scale, and what was rejected on the way. It is the reasoning, and it is the reason this block is long.

attrs.description: facts about the device that belong to no view, filed by section. Keys are globally unique across sections and keep their own prefix (`power.power-max-w`, not `power.max-w`): each one is flattened onto the SVG root as `data-<key>`, where it is read without its container, and the section is a classification of a fact rather than a namespace for it - so re-filing a key changes no drawing and no export. Lint L25 is an error if two sections claim one key. The profiles vocabulary states what each device class owes in terms of these sections.

physical.description: the box as an object: weight, and anything dimensional the chassis block does not already hold. `rack: '13 RU'` beside `chassis.ru: 13` is NOT physical data, it is the same fact written twice - the structured one is the one a tool can use

performance.description: what the box forwards and on what: capacity, forwarding rate, buffers, table sizes, the modes its cages run and the optics they take

power.description: what it draws and what it is fed. `power-max-w`, `power-typical-w`, `power-min-w`, suffixed `-ac-w`/`-dc-w` only where the vendor states both and they differ. These are the WHOLE BOX's spellings and are refused on a component contract (lint L28); a module says `power-draw-max-w` or `power-output-w`, which is what stops a sum over a chassis's occupants resolving to a plausible wrong number

power-envelope.description: what the vendor's own figure COVERS, where a document says - and it is what decides whether a module total may be reconciled against that figure at all. Casa states '3.6 kW per fully loaded chassis'; Cisco publishes no chassis draw for the ASR9000 at all, only a per-card table and an instruction to compute your own budget. The same key on two chassis can therefore mean opposite things, and without this word a consumer cannot tell which it is holding. An enum rather than a free string because a value that licenses a reconciliation drifts into `fully-loaded`, `full` and `yes`. ABSENT means nobody has looked; `unstated` means somebody read the datasheet and it is silent, which is a finding - the same distinction `lifecycle.eol: none-announced` draws

input-plug.description: THE INPUT POWER PORT TYPE of a rack PDU, as a slug: the DCIM power-port type of the part its outlets are `fed-by` (`nema-l21-30p`, `cs8365c`, `iec-60320-c20`). Lint L167 fails when the two differ. The cord, its length and gauge go in `input-cord` and the provenance.

input-cord.description: whether a rack PDU's input cord is fixed to it or plugs into an inlet.

input-phase.description: a rack PDU's input, single-phase or three-phase. With `three`, an outlet's `lines` decide its DCIM `feed_leg` (lint L169 warns where they are unstated).

input-wiring.description: a three-phase input's wiring; absent when single-phase (lint L167). A line-to-neutral outlet on a `wye` input is the only outlet that exports a `feed_leg`.

input-voltage-v.description: a rack PDU's nominal input voltage as a number, as a source states it; line to line when three-phase. A PDU states its voltage here and in the prose `input-ac`, and not in `input-voltage` (lint L168 warns on both).

input-current-a.description: a rack PDU's rated input current, derated, in amperes - the figure the drawings give (24 A on a 30 A plug).

plug-rating-a.description: what a rack PDU's input plug is rated for, in amperes, where it differs from `input-current-a` - the figure the SKU titles give.

capacity-kw.description: the load a rack PDU can hand on, in kilowatts - NEVER a draw: the profile's draw requirement is not met by it. A `capacity-scope` sentence qualifies it where a source does.

thermal.description: operating temperature and the machinery that holds it - fans, airflow. `operating-temp-f2b` and `operating-temp-b2f` are two facts, not two spellings: the airflow SKUs have different ranges

environmental.description: conditions the box is rated for but does not control - storage temperature, humidity, altitude

platform.description: what it is built from: ASIC, CPU, memory, storage, flash, BMC, external TCAM, the software it ships with

features.description: capabilities that are switched on rather than dimensioned - MACsec, PoE, FlexE, timing, TPM, GNSS. Where a datasheet says 'optional' the fact may belong in `configurations` as a SKU variant instead; state it here only while the SKUs are unmodelled

management.description: how it is operated and observed: management ports, firmware bundles, telemetry the box exposes about itself

metering-scope.description: A RACK PDU'S METERING, the finest level it meters: `none`, `input`, `branch` (each breaker or bank, and the input) or `outlet` (each outlet, each branch and the input). Each level includes every level above it, so one word carries three columns. Stated with `outlet-switching`, never alone (lint L166); the two derive the published class (`pdu-class` in configs.json and devices.json), which is never stated.

outlet-switching.description: A RACK PDU'S OUTLET SWITCHING: true when an outlet can be switched on and off. Stated with `metering-scope` (lint L166). With true every outlet declares the `[on, off]` state vocabulary (a warning naming each that does not); with false no outlet declares one (an error).

compliance.description: what it is certified or tested to. Wording is load-bearing and must survive verbatim: 'NEBS Level 3 (pre-test; certificate by request)' is a materially different claim from 'NEBS Level 3', and flattening it would be a false statement about a product

lifecycle.description: GA is assumed. Record only what the vendor has ANNOUNCED, with the link

eol.description: ABSENT means nobody has looked. `none-announced` means somebody searched and the vendor has announced nothing - a real finding, and it must not be indistinguishable from nobody looking. `announced` owes `eol-announcement`

eol-announcement.description: URL of the notice. A date with no link is a claim about a product that no reader can check

other.description: the long tail: a real device fact that fits no section yet. Not an escape hatch - lint L24 counts it and the gaps register carries it as `attrs-unclassified`, so it shrinks as patterns emerge or stays visibly unshrunk

depth.description: millimetres, front face to rear face

ru.description: rack units, for a device that bolts to the rack - `mount` `rack` (the default), `rack-face` or `rack-side`. For a rack-face part it is the units its ears span, and for a rack-side part the units of height it runs beside, not units either occupies. L125: these three state it, and a device mounted any other way does not.

mount.description: HOW THE BOX IS INSTALLED, which a DCIM device type has to know and the dimensions do not say. `rack` is the default and needs no statement; a device mounted any other way says so here and states no `ru`, and the DCIM export then writes `u_height: 0` and `is_full_depth: false` rather than inventing a rack unit. `din-rail` is a box that clips onto a rail (IEC 60715), `wall` one that screws to a surface, `desktop` one that stands on its feet. A box that does more than one names the way it is drawn and exported, and its provenance says the rest. `rack-face` is a part that bolts to rack holes at a rack unit ON THE RAIL FACE, with its body projecting outward from the mounting plane rather than in between the posts - a lacer panel in front of a patch panel. It states `ru` (the units its ears span), its `depth` is that outward projection, and it exports `u_height: 0` like the others because it occupies none. It says nothing about front or rear: the same part goes on either face, and that is a placement's to say. `rack-side` is a part that attaches to the SIDE OF A RACK'S UPRIGHT and runs vertically beside it, outside the rails - a full-height vertical cable manager on its brackets. It states `ru`, the rack units of height it spans, and exports `u_height: 0` and `is_full_depth: false` because it occupies none; it is drawn as it stands, so its front is taller than it is wide (L152), and which side of the rack it stands on is a placement's to say. The name says where on the rack the part attaches; "zero-U" says only what it does not use, and is as true of a vertical power strip. L125 checks it against `ru`.

shell.description: WHAT THE BODY IS MADE OF, for a part that is not a box. Absent, the chassis is a solid box and each view is one of its sides. `sheet` is bent sheet metal: the views are drawn with no housing filled in behind them, and they are ELEVATIONS - in 3D nothing is built from the six faces, because a front view of a tray shows ears and rings that do not lie in the front plane. The solid is what the views' parts build: the floor of a well, which in a sheet body has nothing round it, and whatever stands on that floor or proud of a face. L127 holds it to `thickness`.

thickness.description: millimetres, the gauge of a `shell: sheet` body, as its datasheet states it. A fact about the part and not an instruction to the drawing: each plate's thickness in 3D is its own part's relief. Stated only with `shell: sheet` (L127).

full-depth.description: WHETHER A RACK DEVICE TAKES BOTH FACES of the rack units it spans, the fact NetBox and Nautobot write as `is_full_depth` and use to decide whether the opposite face of those units is free. A `rack` device is full depth unless it says `false` here: a cable manager 87 mm deep in front of the rails leaves the rear face of its unit free for another part. Stated, not derived from `depth`, because a threshold would quietly re-file every shallow box already imported. Only on a `rack` device (L125); any other mount exports `false`.

overhang.description: HOW FAR REAL PARTS REACH BEYOND THE RACK FACE, in millimetres each side. A `rack` device is drawn between its ear folds, and nothing could stand outside them; some rack hardware has parts that do - the FS CMH-6DR1U bolts a steel end ring to the front of each ear, reaching 43 mm past the 482.6 mm rack width to hold a vertical run beside the posts. Such a device draws its front at the rack-face width with the ears drawn, holding what they carry (as the R740xd does), and a part beyond the face is an ordinary placement at negative x or past the view's width. This states the envelope, so the reach is a claim and not an accident of an `at`: L150 refuses a part outside its view that the side's figure does not cover, and L151 warns when no part reaches a stated figure. `left` and `right` are as seen from the front. Only on a `rack` device (L125). Neither DCIM schema has a field for it; the export writes it as a comment.

ears.description: WHERE THE EARS ARE AND WHERE THEY CAN PUT THE FACEPLATE, for a rack device. Two spellings. The bare string `behind`: the mounting flanges sit behind the body, so a front 482.6 mm wide is the body's own width and not ears drawn by mistake - the FS USCMH-SFDABSB2U is a duct as wide as the rack, standing in front of the rails on flanges folded back behind it; L43, which warns that a 480-487 mm face is a rack face with its ears on, stands down. The object says the same with `behind: true`, and adds what the ears span (`h`, `y`) and the named `positions` the device can be mounted at. configs.json always publishes the object. Only on a `rack` device (L125).

behind.description: the bare string `behind` as a key: the flanges fold back behind a body as wide as the rack, so the face is the part. `{behind: true}` stands L43 down as the bare string does.

h.description: millimetres, the height the ears span, when it is not the chassis height (a 13U box with 10U ears). The device still occupies its `ru`. Absent, the ears run from `y` to the top of the chassis. The generic L-bracket ear is drawn this tall; lint L164 warns when `y + h` reaches above the chassis.

y.description: millimetres, the bottom of the ears above the bottom of the chassis, when `h` is less than the chassis height; 0 when absent

color.description: the ears' colour, a fill as `chassis.color` is written, when they are not silver. The generic L-bracket ear is drawn in it; absent, it is silver (#c8cacc), because most network gear has bare or plated steel ears even when its faceplate is black. A colour and not a dimension: the device lock hashes it with the rest of `ears` under chassis surface, so stating or changing it is a patch.

positions.description: THE NAMED PLACES THE EARS CAN PUT THE FACEPLATE. Manuals name positions far more often than they measure them, so `name` is required and `at` is not: a figure the source does not state is not written. At most one position is the `default` (L160), and no two have the same `name` and `label` (L165): two of one name are told apart by their labels.

name.description: `flush`: the faceplate in the plane of the rails; `recessed`: behind them; `proud`: in front of them; `mid`: a mid-mount on a two-post frame; `rear`: ears at the back, bolted to the rear rails

label.description: the vendor's own words for the position ("transponder flush")

at.description: millimetres from the front of the faceplate back to the plane the ears bolt to, positive when the ears are behind the faceplate: -25.4 puts the faceplate 25.4 behind the rails, 0 is flush, 228 a mid-mount 228 in front of a two-post frame. Measured on the device, not in a rack. Written only when a figure or a drawing gives it.

default.description: the position the device ships in. At most one position says it (L160).

racks.description: the rack types the source restricts this position to; absent, any. The schema holds the words (L1).

part.description: the kit part this position needs when it is not the ears that ship (the Smartoptics mid-mount part): `kit` is the ref of a kit this device lists under `chassis.kits`, and `part` the `id` of one of that kit's parts (L162)

kits.description: THE RAIL, BRACKET AND SLIDE KITS THIS DEVICE TAKES, each a `kind: kit` in the library. A kit is shared - one rail serves a dozen chassis - so it is modelled once and named here, never copied and never placed (L5). The site defaults to the `in-box` kit, then to the first listed. Only on a `rack` device (L125). configs.json carries each kit resolved inline.

ref.description: a `kind: kit` in the library, namespace/name@major, listed once (L161)

supply.description: `in-box`: shipped with the device; `optional`: sold separately

variant.description: `reversed`: the kit mounts the device back to front, ports to the hot aisle

depth.description: OVERRIDES THE DEPTH OF ONE CONFIGURATION OF THE KIT FOR THIS DEVICE: the same rail can have a different minimum on another chassis group. `config` names a configuration `id` of the kit, and `range` replaces that configuration's `depth` whole, so it has the same shape - one `[min, max]`, or one range for each hole type the configuration gives (L163).

bevel.description: EDGES CUT BACK AT 45 DEGREES, for a housing that is not a plain box. Each entry names edges by the two faces that meet at them - `front-left`, `top-right`, `rear-bottom`; order does not matter - and the millimetres the bevel takes off each of those two faces. The front of an AurCore AIS switch is narrower than its body because the edges where it meets the finned sides are bevelled: `{edges: [front-left, front-right], size: 11}`. The face drawings keep their full size and their coordinates: a bevel along a view's line of sight cuts a corner off its outline, and a bevel on one of its own edges is drawn as a strip beside the flat face, which is where parts go. The build makes the solid from it; L126 checks it.

size.description: millimetres taken off each of the two faces - one number for a 45-degree bevel, or a pair [a, b] taking a off the first face named and b off the second (`top-left: [11, 16]` takes 11 off the top and 16 off the left)

airflow.description: WHERE AIRFLOW LIVES. The chassis is the home; a configuration states `airflow` only when it DIFFERS from this, and the build reads the configuration first and falls back here. The enums differ on purpose: `side` and `passive` are chassis answers a configuration cannot give, because a fanless enclosure and a side-breathing modular chassis offer no airflow option to choose between. L91 checks the division.

power.description: WHAT THE BOX IS FED WITH, stated the way `airflow` is: the chassis is the home, and a configuration states `power` only when its build DIFFERS - which, unlike airflow, is the usual case, because most switches are sold as an AC and a DC build of one chassis. So a box with one feed says it here once (`power: dc` on a fixed -48 V router), and a box with an AC and a DC build says it on each configuration and not here. `<device>.configs.json` publishes each build's resolved answer as `configs[].power`, and `options.power` there and in devices.json is the union across the builds a buyer can order - what a tool filtering by feed reads instead of parsing `ac`/`dc` out of a configuration name or `input-dc` out of attrs. L118 checks the division; L119 asks for it where a device has supplies and says nothing.

edge.description: faceplate EDGE COLOUR - the stroke drawn around the housing rect, defaulting to #22262a. A colour and not a dimension, so the device lock hashes it under `surface`: recolouring an edge moves nothing, and is a patch.

configurations.description: renderable variants: bay population, skin choices, airflow/region context. EACH ONE SAYS WHAT KIND OF THING IT IS (`kind`), so a consumer can tell an orderable SKU from an illustration, and an illustration (`example`) never exports as a DCIM device type.

default.description: the configuration a viewer opens with. Where a `base` exists it is the default and nothing else may claim it, so `default` never means 'whatever the drawing happens to be populated with'.

airflow.description: ONLY WHEN THIS BUILD DIFFERS FROM THE CHASSIS. A front-to-back and a back-to-front SKU of one switch are two configurations of one chassis, and that is what this is for; a chassis whose airflow does not depend on the build states it once under `chassis.airflow` instead. Restating the chassis value here is what L91 reports. Narrower than the chassis enum on purpose: `side` and `passive` are not options a buyer picks between.

power.description: ONLY WHEN THIS BUILD DIFFERS FROM THE CHASSIS - see `chassis.power`. An AC and a DC build of one switch are two configurations of one chassis, and each says which it is here; a box with one feed states it once on the chassis instead, and restating it here is what L118 reports. It must agree with the supplies the build seats: `dc` over a bay holding an `-ac` supply is L120.

occupants.description: what is PLUGGED IN, keyed by the id of the receptacle it plugs into. A populated port is not a different port - it is the same cage with an optic in it - so this is a configuration the way `bays` is, and a device can be drawn bare or fitted without either being a separate model. Sugar for a `mate-to` placement: the occupant is positioned by its `mate` connection point landing on the host's, and L12 holds the two to the same `interface`, so nothing here is a second positioning path. The value is a component ref, or a mapping carrying `ref` and an explicit `id` where the derived `<host>-occupant` is not the name you want on the row

turn.description: HOW FAR THE OCCUPANT IS TURNED ON ITS SEAT, in degrees, RELATIVE TO THE SEAT: added after the host's own turn and any axis a spanning host's pair runs on. One of the turns the host allows - its interface's `turns` in the connectors vocabulary, narrowed by its presented point's own; an interface naming none allows 0 alone, and lint L146 fails on a value outside the list. A ring lug on a ground stud turns freely, so the direction its wire leaves in is the installer's choice and this states it. Left out, the build computes the default (down, toward the nearer side edge, the other side, up - the first that crosses no part, bay or other seat) and publishes it as `seat-turns` in configs.json.

bays.description: what is seated, keyed by bay id, overriding that bay's own `default`. AN EMPTY STRING MEANS THE BAY IS EMPTY - it is how a `kind: base` empties the traffic slots while leaving supplies, fans and engines seated, and the renderer draws it as a real hole with the depth of what the bay accepts rather than a black rectangle painted on the panel.

part-numbers.description: orderable SKUs for this configuration: model -> {part, power-cord}

bay-attrs.description: bay path -> attrs for the occupant seated THERE: `psu-1: {watts: 750W}` prints on that supply alone, where `component-attrs` reaches every instance of a component. A nested path - `riser-1/slot-1` - reaches a module's own bay. The keys are the occupant's `fields`, and the values print on its `data-from` nodes.

component-attrs.description: component name OR placement/bay id -> extra data-* attrs for this configuration. A component name reaches every instance of that part and is how a configuration says which FRU model or part number is fitted; a PLACEMENT OR BAY ID reaches exactly one, and is how it says something true of that instance alone. The two compose, the instance winning. The ASR 9001-S is the same metal as the 9001 with two of its four SFP+ ports disabled until a licence is applied: both draw six `std/sfp-ganged`, so `{sfp-ganged: ...}` marks all six, and keying the two placement ids marks only the two that are meant. `bays` and `only-in` say what is THERE; this says what is TRUE of it. L94 checks the key resolves, because a key that matches nothing is silently ignored.

kind.description: `base`: the chassis with enough in it to power on and log in - supplies, fans and the routing or supervisory engines populated, TRAFFIC SLOTS EMPTY. On a fixed one-RU switch that is the fans plus one power flavour. At most one per device, and it is the default: what you spec first is a chassis you can reach, before deciding what goes in it. `orderable`: a SKU of this same device - power feed, airflow, region. Named EXPLICITLY even when the base already embodies one of them, so that asking for the DC variant does not mean knowing which flavour the base happens to be. Exports as a device type. `example`: an illustrative population - a redundancy scheme, a worked configuration. Renders as a picture, and NEVER names or creates a device type, because it is not a thing anyone can order. `model`: this configuration is really a different product - the MX80's mx5/mx10/mx40, the ASR-9001-S. Flagged rather than solved: these most likely want to become devices of their own, and until they do this at least stops them reading as variants of one chassis.

source.description: where this configuration comes from. A `base` is either DERIVED - built from the group roles, populating everything `service` and `management` and blanking everything `traffic` - or SOURCED, when the vendor publishes the configuration as an orderable bundle and the library should follow it rather than invent one. Juniper publishes MX10016-BASE and MX10016-PREMIUM with their exact component counts; Cisco and Casa do not, for the chassis here. The two are not equally good and a consumer should be able to tell them apart, which is what this says.

views.description: which panel each face wears in this configuration, as {face: view name}. Faces not named fall back to the view named after them, so a configuration that overrides only the front keeps the standard rear and sides. THIS IS WHAT COUPLES THE FACES: a front and a rear that do not go together on real hardware cannot both be named here, so the impossible machine has nowhere to live. Scoping a bay with `only-in` cannot do that - it varies occupants within one panel and says nothing about any other face.

groups.description: every `group:` used in any view, declared once: the vendor's word for one of them (term), where numbering starts, and shared attrs. Lint L17 rejects an undeclared group

role.description: what this block is FOR - the one thing the drawing cannot work out for itself. A PSU bay, a fan bay and a line-card bay are all data-class `bay`, the same hole with a module in it, so anything ranking the tree by class cannot tell which of them is why the box exists and which two keep it alive. Only the group knows. `traffic` is the work the device is bought to do - line-card slots and the ports that carry user traffic. `fabric` is the cell or chassis interconnect of a distributed chassis - the ports on a DDC or VDR line-card box that lead to its fabric boxes, and every port on the fabric box itself. PORTS ONLY: it is not a customer port, which is `traffic`, and it is not a fabric CARD, which is a control-plane board in `service` below; an exporter still lists these ports as interfaces, because they are cabled like any other. It is its own bucket so that a filter on `traffic` means the ports a customer plugs into, and so that one on `fabric` finds the interconnect on every such box, whatever the vendor called the bank. `management` is how you reach and discipline it - the OOB jack, the console, the craft port, the timing and sync interfaces; a bucket of its own, so that a tree ordered by role never puts a console socket among the traffic ports. `service` is what keeps it running - PSUs, fans, filters, power shelves, AND THE CONTROL-PLANE CARDS: routing engines, route processors, supervisors, fabric and switch-control boards. A control-plane card is not `traffic`, which a base configuration empties, and an RE is not `management`: that bucket is jacks and ports, the things you plug into, not the cards behind them. `indicator` is what you read - LEDs, displays. `furniture` is what you neither connect to nor read - ears, rivets, labels, grounding points, doors. Ordering WITHIN a role stays document order, which already reads correctly; this only says which bucket the block falls in. Lint L37 checks it.

physical-context.description: Redfish PhysicalContext value shared by everything in this block, e.g. 'PowerSupply' for the PSU bays. A whole group is the natural place to say it once

mixed.description: the job these ports do together, when they do NOT share a media or a speed and that is deliberate: a management cluster of SFP+, USB and RJ45, a timing block of RJ45 and coax. The default shape of a port group is one family - one media, one speed - because that is what lets the block declare its facts once in `attrs`; a group spanning families is normally a bucket nobody has sorted yet, and lint L23 says so. This field is the author's answer: the vendor's faceplate calls these one thing, and splitting them by media would be a worse drawing. State the function, e.g. 'management cluster' or 'timing inputs and outputs' - it is a reason, not a switch, and L23 also objects if it is set on a group that is in fact one family

states.description: what this indicator's states MEAN on this device. Overrides the component's own vocabulary, which can only be generic - the same led-dot is a speed lamp on one port and a link lamp on the next. A block of eighteen speed lamps shares one vocabulary and says it once; a placement inside it may still override

oneOf.description: per contracted element, when one component carries two lamps that do NOT share a vocabulary - a management jack whose left lamp is green for 1G and whose right is amber for 10M/100M. Keys are element ids of the referenced component; lint L20 rejects one that names no element

description.description: the vendor's own sentence about this block of indicators, kept beside the tokens

additionalProperties.description: one face of the device, written in the order the part is made: size the panel, say whether it is an open frame, punch it, print it, populate it. Key order is linted (L16).

empty.description: this face was LOOKED FOR AND IS NOT DOCUMENTED, and this says where you looked. Without it a face with nothing on it is indistinguishable from a face nobody got to, so the capability check counts it as unfinished and the only way to pass would be to draw something - which on an undocumented face means inventing it. Prose rather than a boolean, and long enough that a bare `empty: yes` will not validate, because the claim being made is about a search rather than about the drawing. A view declaring this must actually be bare (L60); if a source turns up, the sentence goes and the feature is drawn.

size.description: view dimensions in mm when not the chassis front elevation (e.g. top = width x depth)

open-frame.description: THIS FACE'S BAYS OPEN INTO ONE SHARED INTERIOR, not into a pocket each. An open-frame chassis - card-guide rails top and bottom, a mid-plane, and nothing between the slots, as on the CommScope CH3000 - is seen straight through wherever a slot is empty, front to rear. Without this every empty bay compiles to a pocket as deep as its deepest occupant, with four walls, a floor and a back, and the chassis reads in 3D as a row of closed tubes. With it EVERY bay on the face, occupied or not, compiles to a see-through mouth flagged `data-open-frame` - the kit punches it and builds no walls, floor or back round it - and the face's root carries `data-open-frame`, which tells the kit to line the inside of the box so the interior reads as the chassis's. A seated module is drawn over its mouth as usual, and pulling it leaves the frame open rather than a dark box. Declare it on every face whose slots open into the interior (a mid-plane chassis: front and rear).

panel.description: the sheet metal - what it is (decor) and where it is punched (cutouts)

pattern.description: `brush` is a brush strip: bristles closing an opening that cables pass through. Unlike the other patterns it paints itself as a solid field - the bristles and the dark between them - so it needs no backing rect, and it is never an air aperture. In 3D it is opaque wherever it is drawn; on a sheet body give it `sink` for the depth of the plate it fills, and it is built as a slab there. Say which way the bristles run with `bristle`

bristle.description: with `pattern: brush`: which way the bristles run across the opening, as drawn on this face. Vertical bristles meet in a horizontal line

vent.description: air vent: this decor is a hole through the sheet, this many mm deep - the dark cells of a pattern, or the whole rect when plain-fill. It is the declaration, with `pattern: vent`, that says paint is an opening (the drawing carries it as data-aperture="air"): lint reads it for parts and legends on air, and in 3D the opening is also shown on the inner side of an interior well wall that lies against this face. The depth itself is not built - a vent is painted on both sides of the sheet, not punched

pattern-offset.description: shift the pattern phase under this rect (align lattice rows across corners)

pattern-pitch.description: this rect's pattern tile in mm, w x h. Without it the face gets the pattern's own tile - `slots-h` is 14 x 8, one vendor's louvre pitch - so a bezel with eight rows of louvres in 25mm could only be drawn with three. Pair it with `pattern-offset` to put the lattice's first cell on the rect's own corner

id.description: name this rect in the drawing. Without one it is numbered by kind, and somebody opening the SVG in an editor finds an anonymous rectangle they can only identify by clicking it and watching what highlights

kind.description: what this rect IS - port-shell, recess, label-plate, bezel. A vent field and a stroked outline name themselves from `pattern` and `stroke`; everything else is an unlabelled grey box unless the author says otherwise. It reaches the drawing as data-kind, so the file can be READ rather than clicked through

out.description: decor protrudes this many mm from the face in 3D (raised stampings)

lift.description: standoff: the raised decor STARTS this many mm off the face, so it spans lift..out instead of 0..out. Without it `out` can only build a solid block from the panel outward, which is wrong for anything with a section - a cable-management hook is a thin plate at the FRONT of a horizontal foot, an L rather than a cube. The same key as `lift` on `relief.features`.

source.description: where precisely, in one phrase. Start with '<ns>/<name>@<major>' when the number came from another part, so the claim can be resolved rather than only read.

sink.description: decor is recessed this many mm into the face in 3D (pressed grooves)

fill.description: plain fill (e.g. groove colour) when no pattern

stroke.description: outline-only decor (fibre channels etc.); fill defaults to none

rotate.description: text decor rotation in degrees about its anchor

shape.description: outline of the painted patch. `rect` (with optional `rx`) is the default; `d-sub` is the D-subminiature outline of TE 114-40010 Figure 3 and `slot` a stadium. THE SAME VOCABULARY A CUTOUT'S `shape` TAKES, because paint printed around a connector takes the connector's shape - a patch behind a D-sub is not a rectangle. `circle` is accepted for symmetry and still draws as a rect; decor has `rx`.

depth.description: mm the hole runs into the chassis. Without it a cutout is painted dark and nothing more; with it the 3D kit builds a recess this deep and lays whatever is drawn inside the hole on its floor. A cutout a bay's `rear:` names is a PASSAGE instead: walls only, no floor, so the module's own body stands in it and an empty slot is open through to the front.

wall.description: colour of the recess walls, with `depth`

empty.description: a hole with deliberately nothing in it (a blanked-off option). Without this, a cutout no placement sits in is a lint finding

rotate.description: degrees to turn the aperture about its own centre. A `d-sub` or `slot` hole has a direction, and the part that fills it already says which - the placement's own `rotate`; this turns the hole to match, so a turned connector does not sit in an unturned hole with the corners its aperture does not have showing as ink.

passes.description: PASS-THROUGHS: where cables can cross this face to the opposite side - a brush window, an open hole in a cable manager's wall. Compiled to an invisible `data-class="pass"` rect on the drawing, which is how every consumer reads depth; the DCIM exports ignore it, and nothing routes cables through it yet. L136 keeps it on the face and off the parts; L137 keeps a `cover: brush` and the brush decor drawn over it in step.

shape.description: `obround` is a stadium: the short sides are half circles

cover.description: what closes the opening: nothing, or a brush strip drawn over it as `pattern: brush` decor (L137)

silkscreen.description: Printed matter on the CHASSIS panel. Painted after the panel and its decor and BEFORE components, because on the real device the silkscreen goes down on the punched panel and the modules are installed on top of it. A legend that a module would cover is therefore invisible here, which is the correct behaviour: on the hardware it would be invisible too. Silkscreen printed on a MODULE's own faceplate belongs in that component's skin, inside <g id="silkscreen">, and travels with it.

id.description: optional stable id; needed only when something else refers to this mark

text.description: printed legend. Multi-line uses \n. Exactly one of text or path

fill.description: ink colour; defaults to chassis silk

for.description: what this mark annotates. One placement or bay, or a list when the mark joins things - a leader line from a breaker to its terminal names both. Emitted as data-for. Printed ink annotates something on the face it is printed on: a bare id in this view, never another view and never the chassis.

path.description: printed line or symbol as an SVG path in view mm - a leader line, a polarity arrow, an earth mark. Exactly one of text or path

filled.description: this path ENCLOSES ink rather than tracing a route. A leader line is stroked; a solid arrowhead is filled. Without it every symbol is an outline held shut by its own stroke width, which leaves a pinhole in anything small and cannot be scaled - at twice the size the hole is four times as obvious

fill-rule.description: evenodd where a filled mark has a hole in it - a bored nut, a ring

components.description: what is installed into the panel. bays are things that come out; placements are things that do not

only-in.description: THE CONFIGURATIONS IN WHICH THIS PART OF THE METAL EXISTS AT ALL, which is a different question from what goes in it. Absent means every configuration, which is almost always the answer. A C40G ordered for AC has ONE bolted panel across the bottom rear where a DC chassis has two power-entry openings - not two empty openings, different sheet metal - so the panel is scoped to the AC configurations and the openings to the DC ones; without this a configuration could vary only its OCCUPANTS, and an AC rear would show two empty power-entry bays a DC module could be offered for. Scoping lives HERE, on the bay or placement, rather than in the configuration block, because it is a statement about GEOMETRY and geometry is what a view holds - a configuration says what is fitted, not where the holes are. Distinct from `optional`, which is a build-time flag that hides a part from every configuration at once. Lint L41 checks it.

opening.description: the HOLE IN THE SHEET METAL, when it differs from `size`. `size` is the space the slot RESERVES - what the occupant is placed into and checked against - and on a card cage that is the card including its ejector brackets. The hole the card's plate covers is smaller, and it is the hole you see when the bay is empty. On an ASR 9006 they are 395.70 and 352.59: painting the reserved space dark would put 21.5 mm of opening over metal at each end. Absent means the two are the same, which is the common case. Measured only - never inferred from the occupant.

physical-context.description: Redfish PhysicalContext value, e.g. 'PowerSupply', 'Fan', 'NetworkingDevice'. This is the join between the drawing and a running box: it is what lets an ENTITY-MIB entPhysicalTable row or a Redfish Thermal sensor be laid over the bay it actually describes. The `wired` capability flag is exactly 'every bay and every port group says this'

default.description: ref populated by default config; null = open

rotate.description: degrees to rotate the occupant, e.g. a line card mounted horizontally in one chassis and vertically in another

mirror.description: flip the occupant horizontally about its own centre line; handedness, not rotation - a riser whose cards face the other way

plan.description: WHERE THIS BAY'S OCCUPANT IS SEEN FROM ANOTHER FACE. A riser is seated in its rear bay and stands inside the chassis; with the lid off, the top view should show it there. The occupant's contract names the component that draws it from above (`plan.ref`), and this says which view that lands in and where - the plan's top-left in that view's mm. `in:` and `under:` are the target view's, so the plan sits in its well and paints under the lid. `mirror` flips it, for a riser whose cards face the other way, and `rotate: 180` turns it for a module seated in the front. The occupants of the occupant's own bays come along at the offsets those bays declare. The result is a PROJECTION: it carries `data-of` naming the seated part and no data-path of its own, so the tree lists the part once, selecting either face marks both, and the 3D kit builds nothing from it - the body already stands there.

rotate.description: half a turn, for a module seated in a FRONT bay: its plan is drawn face-at-the-top, as a rear-seated module lies, and a front-seated one faces the other way. The plan turns in place and the occupants of its own bays are offset from the opposite corner.

rear.description: WHERE THIS BAY'S OCCUPANT IS SEEN FROM BEHIND, through an open back. The occupant's contract names what draws its back (`faces.rear`); this says which view that lands in and which of that view's panel `cutouts` it is seen through. WHERE in the cutout is not the bay's to say: the back of a module is the back of its body, so it lands where the SEATED occupant's own `body.footprint` stands, mirrored across the bay since it is seen from behind - x = cutout x + (bay w - footprint x - footprint w), y = cutout y + footprint y (the whole face when there is no footprint). A cassette and an adapter panel in the same bay put their backs in two different places. HOW IT IS TURNED is not the bay's to say twice: a bay with `rotate` shows its occupant's back turned by the same angle the other way round (a clockwise turn seen from the front reads anticlockwise from behind), about the hole's centre, with the footprint found in the bay's unturned box - so the cutout of a turned bay is the bay's own turned box, mirrored. The projection is drawn INSIDE the cutout for the 2D rear; in 3D the cutout is a passage and the module's own body, its back painted with the same face, stands in it at its real depth. Like `plan:`, the result is a PROJECTION: `data-of`, no data-path, and nothing built from it. The cutout must declare a `depth` (L72).

floor.description: mm below the face at which this bay's occupant STANDS, when that is not the well's own floor. With `in:` alone a module stands on the well's floor and rises its own height; a card in a riser stands on its slot, and the three slots of a riser are three shelves at three heights inside one well. So a bay may say where its shelf is: the R740xd's riser 1 slots are 26.6, 44.8 and 64.6 down, from the model's seated cards. Only meaningful with `in:`, and never deeper than the well (L13).

in.description: the WELL this bay opens in - a placement in this view drawn as a recess. The module that fills it STANDS ON THE WELL'S FLOOR and rises to its own `size.d`: the bay's plane sits that far above the floor and the body reaches down to it. A 26.1 mm drive in the mid tray, whose floor is 31.31 down, tops out 5.21 below the lid; a 31.3 mm DIMM on the board's PCB, 79.9 down, tops out at 48.6. A well's depth is its floor, never the top of what is in it. Implies the well is `under:` this bay. Checked: the target must be a well in this view.

under.description: Same as on a placement: the ids in this view that lie OVER this bay. A bay is an opening, so it always has somewhere to be under - the R740xd's DIMM sockets sit under the mid-drive tray and its drive bays on the nine configurations that carry one, and the DIMMs' 42.6 mm top clears the tray's 48.89 mm floor. Checked by L13 exactly as a placement's is: the upper part must exist in the view, and the pair is then not compared.

for.description: the placement or bay this one belongs to. A bay is a hole in this face; what it belongs to is on this face too, so a bare id and nothing else. Emitted as data-for.

interface.description: THE INTERFACE THIS SLOT PRESENTS, for an opening whose occupants are not a list anyone published. `accepts` is the vendor's compatibility matrix transcribed - it works because a switch's card catalogue is closed and printed, and the module reference's support tables ARE those lists. An open form factor has no table to transcribe: anyone may build a PCIe card, so a list is unbounded, and one written anyway asserts something the vendor never said. Such a bay names the interface instead and carries no list. Occupants declare the same key via `mates`, exactly as they do for a cage. Deliberately not an enum - a new interface is a new key, not a schema change. Electrical detail (a generation, a lane width) belongs in `attrs`, NOT here: a gen3 card seats in a gen4 slot and an x8 card in an x16, so matching on an exact key would refuse hardware that fits.

items.description: A bay says what goes in it in ONE OF TWO WAYS, and must say it somehow: `accepts` for a closed vendor matrix, `interface` for an open form factor. Both together is fine - a slot can be standard AND have a published list. Neither is a hole that promises nothing.

only-in.description: THE CONFIGURATIONS IN WHICH THIS PART OF THE METAL EXISTS AT ALL, which is a different question from what goes in it. Absent means every configuration, which is almost always the answer. A C40G ordered for AC has ONE bolted panel across the bottom rear where a DC chassis has two power-entry openings - not two empty openings, different sheet metal - so the panel is scoped to the AC configurations and the openings to the DC ones; without this a configuration could vary only its OCCUPANTS, and an AC rear would show two empty power-entry bays a DC module could be offered for. Scoping lives HERE, on the bay or placement, rather than in the configuration block, because it is a statement about GEOMETRY and geometry is what a view holds - a configuration says what is fitted, not where the holes are. Distinct from `optional`, which is a build-time flag that hides a part from every configuration at once. Lint L41 checks it.

interfaces.description: THE INTERFACES THIS PLACEMENT PRESENTS, when it is more than one and is not itself an interface. A Compact SFP (CSFP) module fits a standard SFP cage and carries two independent BiDi fibre connections, each its own switch interface; the switch's silicon has both whether or not a module is seated, and devices here ship unpopulated, so the two belong to the HOST CAGE and are declared on it: `interfaces: [port-1, port-3]`. The DCIM export then emits one interface per id, typed from the cage, and none for the placement. Not breakout: breakout is a MODE a port is configured into and stays a description on one interface, where these are always present and a DCIM must list each. Ids must be unique in the view and not name a placement or bay, and only a port presents interfaces. Lint L105 checks them.

physical-context.description: Redfish PhysicalContext value. See the same key on a bay; declaring it once on the group is usually right, and a placement overrides

optional.description: render only when --with <tag> is given (e.g. ears)

states.description: what this indicator's states MEAN on this device. Overrides the component's own vocabulary, which can only be generic - the same led-dot is a speed lamp on one port and a link lamp on the next

oneOf.description: per contracted element, when one component carries two lamps that do NOT share a vocabulary - a management jack whose left lamp is green for 1G and whose right is amber for 10M/100M. Keys are element ids of the referenced component; lint L20 rejects one that names no element

positions.description: what each position of a part's position fields MEANS on this device: a field key, then each option and its meaning - `sw-3: {on: alarm enabled for breaker position A3, 'off': alarm silenced}`. Documentation carried into the drawing as `data-positions`; it sets nothing, because a position is a field and is set by `attrs`

description.description: the vendor's own sentence about this indicator, kept beside the tokens - 'Blue = 100G, Green = 40G'. Prose, never a state list

mate-to.description: id of a placement in this view to mate into. The renderer positions this component so its `mate` connection-point coincides with the host's, so an occupant never carries hand-computed centring offsets. Mutually exclusive with `at`.

for.description: what this part is bound to - an LED to its port, a button to its module. One target or a list, and a list means collectively: a FAN lamp over five trays names all five. A target in another view of the same device is written 'view/id', because a front-panel PSU lamp indicates a PSU that lives in the rear. The literal 'chassis' names the whole unit, for an indicator with no modelled subject. Emitted as data-for; never inferred from names.

fed-by.description: THE POWER INPUT THIS OUTPUT HANDS ON, for a power outlet on a distribution panel: the id of a placement on this device, in any view, whose part exports a power port. The DCIM export writes it as the outlet's `power_port`, which both NetBox and Nautobot import by name within the same device type. Stated on each placement and never inferred from an `-a`/`-b` in a name. Lint L132 fails when it does not resolve. L134 reports an outlet that states none: a warning at `draft` and `modelled`, an error at `verified`. Stating one is a minor version; changing one re-files an imported outlet's feed and is a major.

through.description: THE POSITION THIS CIRCUIT RUNS THROUGH: the id of a bay on this device, in any view, whose occupant protects it - a breaker or fuse position - OR of a placement of a part of class `breaker`, a breaker fixed to the unit (a rack PDU's branch breaker). It crosses a face (the output is on the rear, the breaker on the front), which `for:` cannot say: `for:` is a UI binding emitted as data-for that waives L13's overlap check, and these two are not near each other. The DCIM export writes it as a sentence on the outlet's description, and on a bay's, because neither target relates an outlet to a module bay; an outlet through a fixed breaker takes that breaker's `lines`. Optional; a panel with fixed, unprotected outputs has none. Stating one is a minor version, changing one a major. Lint L133 fails when it does not resolve. L135 warns when one bay position protects more than one circuit; a fixed PDU breaker feeds many outlets by design, so L135 reads bays only.

lines.description: THE CONDUCTORS A CIRCUIT IS WIRED ACROSS, on the placement that protects it: a part of class `breaker`, or an outlet that has no breaker. `[L1, L2]` is line to line, `[L1, N]` line to neutral. An outlet `through` a fixed breaker takes the breaker's lines instead of restating them. The DCIM export writes them on the outlet's description, and writes `feed_leg` only for a line-to-neutral outlet on a three-phase wye input (L1 is A, L2 B, L3 C). Stating them is a minor version, changing them a major: both move an imported outlet description or `feed_leg`. Lint L169 checks them.

frames.description: ids this part SURROUNDS rather than covers - a frame whose bounding box takes in openings its ink does not. L13 compares boxes, which is right for almost every part and wrong for a frame; this is the declaration that makes the difference checkable instead of assumed. Name only what the openings actually clear. NOT a way to silence a real overlap: a part that genuinely paints over another is an error. Distinct from `behaviour: mounts`, which says a part lies OVER what is behind it and draws after the bays - a drive cage surrounds its drives and must draw BEFORE them, so the two are not interchangeable.

in.description: the WELL this part stands in - a placement in this view drawn as a recess (an unmounted, non-module part with `size.d`). A top view with its lid off is a section, and a part on the floor of a well is not at the face: the R740xd's heatsinks stand on the system board's PCB 79.9 mm down. The renderer sinks the part by the well's depth (a negative z-lift, summed like any other) and its `out` features rise from the floor. Implies the well is `under:` this part for L13 and for paint order, so it need not be repeated. Checked: the target must be a well in this view.

mirror.description: flip this instance horizontally about its own centre line; handedness, not rotation. The same key a bay offers its occupant: the R740xd's riser 3 is riser 1's cage at the other wall, so its card stands with the PCB outboard and the connectors inboard the other way about.

under.description: ids in this view that lie OVER this part - the system board names the shroud and the fan wall that stand on it, the shroud names the lid that closes over it. A faceplate has one height and two parts in one place is a sizing error; a view with its cover off is a section through several, and everything in it overlaps in plan because it is stacked. This is how a placement says which. L13 does not compare a pair one of which is declared under the other, and it CHECKS the claim rather than trusting it: the lower part must be a well (an aperture with `size.d`) or the upper must be `behaviour: mounts`, because otherwise there is no height for the two to be at. NOT a way to silence a real overlap between two flat parts.

inset.description: mm this INSTANCE is mounted behind the panel face. A part's relief says how far it stands proud when its flange bolts to the sheet metal; a connector on a board set back from the faceplate is the same part mounted differently, and this is where that difference belongs - on the placement, not in a second copy of the part. Every protrusion the instance declares is reduced by this much and anything left wholly behind the panel is not drawn.

lift.description: mm this INSTANCE sits proud of the panel face - the mirror of `inset`, and used when the part is bolted not to the sheet metal but to something already standing off it. Every protrusion the instance declares is raised by this much, so the part needs no second copy with fattened numbers - which is what `inset` avoids in the other direction. The same key as `lift` on `relief.features`, on composed `parts:` and on `panel.decor`.

guides.description: WHERE CABLES RUN ALONG THIS FACE, declared rather than read off the drawing. `duct` is a channel walled by fingers: its box on this view, the direction cables run along it, and the pitch and the gap of the fingers along its walls. Nothing consumes it yet: it compiles to an unpainted `data-class="guide"` rect on the face, and the DCIM exports ignore it. A ring that every placement of a part carries is declared on the part's contract as `guide:`, not here. L138 holds a duct inside its view.

run.description: the direction cables run along the channel, across (`x`) or down (`y`) this view

finger-pitch.description: millimetres, centre to centre of the fingers along the run

finger-gap.description: millimetres, the clear gap between two fingers, which a cable is laid through into the channel

face.description: which face this view draws, when the view is not NAMED after one. A view called `front` needs no `face`; a second front - a different panel for the same face, say a 12 x 3.5 inch front beside a 24 x 2.5 inch one - declares `face: front` and is a VARIANT. A variant draws only when a configuration binds it, and draws under the face's name, so a consumer still asks for `front` and gets whichever front that configuration wears.

portfolio.description: where this device sits in the vendor's own catalogue, in the vendor's own words. Free text on purpose: a controlled vocabulary is to be harvested from what accumulates, not designed up front. All fields optional; a device without a portfolio block sorts under its manufacturer.

line.description: the vendor's business line, e.g. 'Service Provider'

family.description: the vendor's word for the category, e.g. 'Aggregation Router'

series.description: marketing series, e.g. 'AGR400'; the model is the SKU root

also-listed-in.description: other catalogue categories the vendor ALSO files this device under, in the vendor's own words. `line` is the category of the vendor's own canonical product URL; this is everywhere else it appears. A consumer filtering by category should union the two, so a box the vendor lists twice shows up in both lists.

interfaces.description: WHAT THE VENDOR'S OWN OPERATING SYSTEM CALLS EACH PORT, for a box that ships with one. The same rules a NOS vendor's listing states: `physical` is a placement id or an id a placement presents, with `{n}` over `range`; `name` is the interface name, with `{n}` or arithmetic on it. The DCIM export of the hardware's own device type names each interface by the rule that names its id, and by the faceplate id where no rule does. Two connectors of one interface take one name and export once. A listing's own `interfaces` still decide that listing's document. The same rules also name the device's power outlets by their printed labels - a rack PDU's `outlet-a1` exports as `A1` - and an outlet no rule names keeps its placement id. Changing a name is a major bump: a DCIM that imported the type holds the old one.

name.description: NOS interface name pattern, e.g. 'swp{n}' or 'Ethernet{(n-1)*4}'

gaps.description: unknowns no rule can ever find, because the manifest looks complete. 'The HIG has no port-lamp table' is a fact about a DOCUMENT, not about this file, and only someone who read the source knows it. Detectable gaps - a port with no media, an indicator with no `for:` - are derived from the lint rules at build time and must NOT be listed here: a hand-kept list of machine-findable problems goes stale the first time someone fixes one. Declare the unknowns, derive the rest.

what.description: the missing knowledge, as a token: port-led-semantics, fan-direction

scope.description: what it applies to: group names, instance ids, or view names

reason.description: why it is missing, because that decides who can close it. `sources-disagree` is the one that is NOT an absence: two documents we hold state different values for one fact. It is common rather than exceptional - a datasheet's maximum power and the same product's quick-start guide, or a figure in a guide's prose and another in its table - and picking the bigger number and saying nothing loses a real finding. The `note` carries both figures with their sources

note.description: what was looked at and what it did not say. Cite the section, so the next reader does not repeat the search

wanted.description: required, and the most valuable field: the difference between 'we don't know' and a request someone can act on

blocks.description: capability flags or levels this gap stands in the way of, so a consumer can join a flag to its explanation structurally rather than by reading the prose in `wanted`. Optional, and an empty list is a fine answer - do not invent a blocker to fill the field. Absent or empty means 'blocks nothing we can name', not 'unknown'.

power-feed.description: a supply feed, in three words: `ac` is mains through an IEC or similar inlet; `dc` is telecom DC, -48 V nominal (-36 to -75 V across the whitebox datasheets); `hvdc` is 240/380 V DC. A build fed by two kinds at once - a fixed box with an AC inlet AND a DC terminal both fitted - lists both, and a list is never used for one.

provenance.description: field name -> where the figure came from. The same shape as the component schema's `provenance`, so a provenance note means one thing whether it is written on a device, a cutout or a placement.

state.description: one state a lamp can be in. The name is a token because `state-<name>` is a CSS class; the sentence explaining it belongs in `description` alongside. The same shape as the component schema's state, so a state means one thing whether it is declared on a part or overridden on a placement.

behavior.description: how the lamp is lit, as opposed to what colour it is lit. Omitted means solid. A state is colour AND behaviour: solid green and blinking green are different facts on real hardware. `rate` is the blink frequency in hertz, because a lamp blinking twice a second and one blinking four times a second are two different documented conditions on the same drive and flattening both to `blinking` throws the distinction away. `sequence` is for a pattern no single colour and rate can express - Dell's drive status lamp blinks green three seconds, amber three seconds, then off for six, which is three phases with durations rather than a blink of anything.

color.description: the second colour, for `alternating` - the lamp flashes between `color` and this one

rate.description: blink frequency in hertz, for `blinking` and `alternating`. Omitted means once a second.

phases.description: for `sequence`: the cycle in order. Each phase names a colour and how long it holds; a phase with NO colour is the lamp off, which is a phase like any other and is how 'blinks green, amber, and turns off' gets said. Durations are seconds and may be omitted, in which case the phases divide the cycle evenly - some vendors give the order without the timing, and recording that as an even division is more honest than inventing durations.

color.description: the colour this phase holds; absent means the lamp is off for it
LED colour for this state, emitted as scoped CSS

for-target.description: what a placement's `for:` names: a bare id, meaning a placement or bay in the same view; 'view/id', meaning one in another view of the same device, because a front-panel PSU lamp indicates a PSU that lives in the rear and only the qualified form can spell that; or the literal 'chassis', the whole unit, for an indicator whose subject is not a modelled part. A list means collectively - a FAN lamp over five trays names all five and belongs to none of them.

confidence.description: where a NUMBER came from. THE SAME VOCABULARY THE COMPONENT SCHEMA USES, so a device's 3D projections say where their figures came from in the same words as a part. The component schema's `confidence` says what each token means; `borrowed` in particular asserts that the named origin MEASURED the magnitude, and lint L36 checks it.

kit-ref.description: a kit's ref, namespace/name@major, as `chassis.kits[].ref` writes it

rack-type.description: a four-post rack or cabinet, a two-post frame, or a two-post frame mounted at its centre: the words a kit configuration's `racks` uses in the component schema

kit-range.description: `[min, max]` in mm, min below max (L157). Inches in the source are converted; the figures as printed stay in provenance.

kit-depth.description: THE RACK DEPTH A KIT CONFIGURATION FITS, front flange to rear flange, in mm: one `[min, max]`, or one range per hole type when the source gives them separately (`square`, `round`, `threaded`). A device's `chassis.kits[].depth.range` overrides it with the same shape.
